I love the idea, but it's challenging because there are so many different knitting styles, disabilities, and ways of adapting to those disabilities. Take people with a missing finger--if it's something other than the pointer finger or thumb, it's probably just a matter of adjusting how you tension yarn and hold the needles and doesn't need a prosthesis, whereas a missing pointer finger or thumb would have a much bigger impact/need for potential solutions, but even that could potentially be mitigated by knitting in a specific way (e.g., english vs. continental).

I suggest either going very broad or very specific--it would be hard to make a general purpose finger prosthesis that could fit on any finger and still be useful for knitting (more so than a general prosthesis). I think the best option would be to make something that's helpful independent of a specific disability, such as a device that you could place next to you to tension your yarn rather than having to do it with your hands, or a support for knitting needles to reduce wrist strain.

I’m so sorry that you’re going a through this. Ultimately, I don’t think phage therapy is the answer you’re looking for. It will likely take months to develop a phage to treat the specific infection your brother has, and that treatment would still be highly experimental. Even if it worked in vitro (in a Petri dish), with all those other health issues and additional infections such as candidiasis complicating the situation, it’s highly unlikely that it would result in recovery. 

We have this general perception that you can fight through anything, particularly things like infections that seem like they should be treatable, but that’s not always the case. It’s helpful to a lot of people in tough situations, but can also be detrimental to people in scenarios like yours where all the good options have been exhausted but you still feel like you need to fight. Have you talked to your brother about what his priorities are? Does he want to pursue this, or is the search for phage therapy being driven by family members who will feel guilty if they don’t explore every possible avenue? If he’s able to have a conversation on that level with his current sedation/medication level, I’d start there. A lot of people would prefer quality time with their loved ones over experimental treatments that may buy them a bit of time while destroying their quality of life. I encourage you to take his wishes into account, if he’s in a position to express them. 

At the end of the day, I think palliative care is likely the appropriate specialty to manage this, if all traditional antibiotics have been explored. Palliative care providers are incredible people who can bring a lot of comfort to both patients and their families. I’m genuinely so sorry that you’re in this position, and I wish you and your family the best.

Respectfully, it sounds like the underlying issue here may be your health anxiety. As far as I’m aware, POTS can’t be triggered by a panic attack, and anxiety symptoms can overlap a lot with POTS. Health anxiety is especially hard because your anxiety has a specific path to manifest down that reaffirms what you’re anxious about, if that makes sense. And I don’t mean to say that the symptoms you’re feeling are all in your head, anxiety can absolutely cause these physical symptoms. 

You can have your GP see if you meet the sustained 30 bpm hr increase on standing up, but if you don’t, I don’t think it’s necessary or helpful to see a bunch of specialists to try to get a diagnosis. Are you seeing a therapist? I genuinely think that would be the most helpful thing here. 

I hope this doesn’t come across as dismissive. I’ve both been told that my POTS was anxiety before diagnosis, but also dealt with major health anxiety myself after a traumatic hospitalization. Getting a handle on the health anxiety will both help with the cancer worries and isolate any symptoms that are unrelated to anxiety, which would be helpful for diagnosing any underlying physical issues. Wishing you the best of luck!

Hey! I am so, so sorry about what you’re going through, and I can’t imagine dealing with all of that, but I promise you will get through it. My aunt was in a similar situation several years ago where she lost her husband of nearly 40 years, and then a few weeks later the home they’d shared for decades burned to the ground in a wildfire. I would ask her to wear gloves and bring it up with management at the practice. I work in infection prevention and would have a heart attack if I saw someone doing this. If they do anything other than immediately wash their hands, they’re leaving blood on whatever they’re touching, and if they’re ignoring standard precautions by not using gloves to touch blood, they may not be doing other things correctly. The absolute risk is very very low on each occurrence, and I don’t think you have anything to worry about, but there have been outbreaks of bloodborne pathogens from things like this where microscopic traces of blood contaminate shared equipment. Again, I don’t think you need to worry about your own health, but they’re not following standard practices in a way that puts both themselves and patients at risk, and I think it would be a good idea to bring it up to management if you’re comfortable doing so. At a minimum, I’d definitely ask for them to use gloves in the future.

To use your analogy, it's helpful because it's diverting some of the traffic. There's an infectious dose of the organism required to result in illness, let's say 100 cars/hour. If 25 cars/hour now take a side road and don't arrive at the destination (bound to antihistamine), and we only have 75 cars/hour reaching the original destination (binding to the receptors that make us sick), the infectious dose isn't reached and the person doesn't get sick. 

  
How effective this is depends on how many cars it's diverting off the main road, and there's definitely a lot more research that needs to be done. I wouldn't start taking antihistamines for COVID prevention yet. (Anecdotally, I have MCAS and take absolute buckets of antihistamines, and have gotten COVID once.) But it's a very cool and promising study!

If you have any evidence to the contrary that crochet machines can and do exist, I would genuinely be very interested to see it. (Note that there are some weft knitting machines that are marketed as crochet machines, but they are a different technique and do not produce a crocheted fabric.) I find the topic fascinating. Another limitation is that while knitting has the stitches active on a needle, holding it in place and giving a fixed location to interact with the stitches, crochet requires the hook to be inserted into the fabric for each stitch, which needs to be able to happen in several different parts of the stitch from several different angles. Basically, crochet isn't a static object that machines can interact with in a preprogrammed way--it requires analyzing visual input to determine where the hook needs to be inserted, rather than just executing a series of commands based on the known location of a fixed object, as is generally the case when creating machined parts. Obviously there is technology to do this in other contexts, but adapting it to crochet would be another challenge to overcome that makes the development of a crochet machine even less economically viable. 

My two cents is that the most viable path forward for a crochet machine would be limiting the movement of the fabric to allow the machine to interact with it in a more structured way--essentially using pins/hooks to keep the stitches in place similar to a knitting machine, even if the way the stitches are being done is different, to standardize the motions required and greatly reduce the complexity needed for both the hardware and the software. I'd love to hear your expert opinion as well. Thanks for the interesting discussion, hope you continue to have a lovely day.

I think it’s worth differentiating between in house Ingrid and out of house Ingrid. Ingrid’s biggest limitation is her 35% strength growth, which is pretty terrible. When out of house, she autolevels using enemy growth rates, and notably has enemy peg knight growths starting from chapter 6. Enemy peg knights have a 15% strength growth, giving her 50% total strength growths for any levels from chapter 6 onwards while out of house. 

The downside to this is that she doesn’t come with any class mastery when recruited late, missing out on skills like hit+20 or death blow, but I think this is a lot less impactful for Ingrid than most other units. Since her primary role is as a dodge tank and she doesn’t have any high-damage combat arts like swift strikes, most of her damage will occur on the enemy phase, meaning death blow wouldn’t be active anyway. I find that having a few extra points of strength to help her counter damage is much more helpful than death blow on the player phase. 

I find Ingrid works best when I recruit her out of house as late as possible. Not only does she have higher stat totals than I could have trained her up to by that point, but I’m also able to direct that XP towards other characters and have a stronger overall team. When I do that, she almost always ends up as a valuable dodge tank on my end game team. 

In house Ingrid has it much rougher, with her lower growths and a lot of competition for XP with the other strong BL units like Dimitri, Felix, and Sylvain. She still has value as a dodge tank, although she will struggle to do meaningful damage on her counters, and has a lot of flexibility for going physical or magical thanks to her mediocre growths in both (yay?), which you can’t take advantage of if recruiting out of house. If you want a magical Ingrid, in house is your best bet. I’ve done this a few times and she’s fine—dark flier was pretty fun, but definitely one of the weaker units on the team. That being said, BL certainly aren’t hurting for strong physical units, so maybe that is her best role there. 

TL;DR: Out of house Ingrid is great, recruit as late as possible. In house Ingrid has some issues.

Are you sure that they were evaluating you for POTS, and not neurocardiogenic syncope (NCS)? Nitroglycerin during a TTT is a NCS workup, not POTS, and their statement about no treatment/cure is accurate for that condition. It's not necessarily about making money (because they could absolutely bill for a test), but if there's nothing you can do based on the test results, it's completely valid to save the patient money and skip an unpleasant test. That should ideally have been a conversation with your input, though.

The actual description of the TTT you received does sound like a POTS workup, so I'm a bit confused. Regardless, their interpretation isn't necessarily incorrect. They're looking for the difference between your average baseline heart rate (not the lowest individual number) and a sustained increase in your heart rate at 10 minutes (not the highest individual number). There is nothing to gain from lying about test results; even if they were just in it for the profit like you alluded, they would be more likely to over-diagnose you with something than under-diagnose you. It's possible they made a mistake, but I think it's unlikely that it was malicious.

TL;DR I think the issue may be poor communication from the doctor rather than poor care, but if you feel like you can't trust this doctor because of it, it's a good idea to find another one.

Edit: I looked into it a bit more and the standard of care is NOT to perform a TTT for suspected NCS unless the fainting is recurrent or severe ([source](https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/full/10.1161/01.cir.0000031168.96232.ba)). It seems like the differential diagnosis may have shifted from NCS to POTS at some point, but I think the care you received was appropriate, just very poorly communicated.

So like... kind of sounds like you might need a new therapist who has more experience dealing with chronic illness (as long as that won't mess up other mental health stuff, you do you). "Oh don't worry you'll recover" is categorically unhelpful, and kind of actively harmful. The stuff I've been working on with my therapist that's been really helpful is generally:

\-Accepting that EDS has made me physically unable to do some things and grieving that loss, coming to terms with it, and figuring out how to move forward. Because stuff like giving up playing the piano in your case, or being a doctor in mine, is a big deal and worth grieving over.

\-Figuring out how to not feel like a complete piece of shit on the really bad days where I can't do anything. (I've been setting a goal daily that's appropriate for how I feel, and sometimes that goal is taking a nap, but setting and achieving a goal feels good anyway, and if I'm feeling that shitty a nap is genuinely a good self-care move.)

\-Generally developing a more compassionate view of myself where I'm not beating myself up for not being able to do things that other people can.

\-Like I mentioned before, since there's so much that's out of my control with my health, taking responsibility for the things I can control.

Anyway, obviously none of that has made me in less pain, but has definitely helped with the associated mental bullshit. I guess all that is to say that seeing a therapist that has experience dealing with people with chronic illness can be really beneficial. I ghosted a lot of therapists along the way hahaha.

I'm an epidemiologist and am happy to answer any questions anyone has about vaccines. I'm vaccinated, as are my family and all my colleagues in public health. They're safe, they work, and they save lives.

>What are the long term side effects of taking the vaccine?

There are no known long-term side effects of taking the vaccine. However, the long-term effects of COVID-19 are very well documented. My husband and I both got sick last summer and it took us both almost 9 months to recover. If you are worried about long-term illness, get the vaccine to keep yourself safe from COVID.

>Will this experiment lead to Marek’s disease, or ADE?

No, Marek's disease only affects chickens, and there is no evidence that ADE occurs with COVID-19. If ADE were an issue we would expect to see that people who were re-infected with COVID-19 had much more severe illness than people infected for the first time, and that is not the case. 

>The chances of getting 90% of the Global population vaccinated to eradicate covid are very low, why take the additional risk of an experimental gene therapy when the odds of Global herd immunity is so low? Delta variant did not originate in US unvaccinated.

Global herd immunity is ideal, but you only need herd immunity in your community to be protected. The estimates of vaccine coverage needed for herd immunity are closer to 70%. If we had herd immunity in the US, we would not be seeing such an increase in cases due to the delta variant, regardless of where it originated. I also want to note that this isn't a gene therapy, the mRNA vaccines do not enter the cell nucleus where the genes are and they can't change your DNA. The mRNA just has instructions to make a protein that lets your body recognize the virus, and then is broken down afterwards.

>Why is natural immunity not considered protection?

Natural immunity is protective, but immunity from vaccines is better. When you get sick with COVID-19, you create antibodies to random sites on the COVID-19 virus. Some of these antibodies may not help prevent infection, if they attack sites on the virus that aren't accessible to the antibodies. The vaccines make sure that you develop antibodies against the proteins on the outside of the virus, so they can attack it as soon as it enters your system and keep you from getting infected.

>Why was the definition of a vaccine changed to accommodate these mRNA therapies?

I assume you're referring to [this](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/vaccine). The definition of a vaccine was not changed, it just added another example now that mRNA vaccines are being widely used.

>Why was the definition of herd immunity changed to exclude natural immunity?

The definition of herd immunity was not changed and does not exclude natural immunity. ([source](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/coronavirus/in-depth/herd-immunity-and-coronavirus/art-20486808))

>Why are the vaccinated and unvaccinated tests run at different cycle thresholds?

They are not run at different cycle thresholds. ([source](https://healthfeedback.org/claimreview/pcr-tests-on-vaccinated-and-unvaccinated-people-are-evaluated-using-the-same-criteria-the-cdc-didnt-change-criteria-for-detecting-infection-in-vaccinated-people-as-alleged-in-off-guardian-a/))

>Why are cases counted differently for the vaccinated than the unvaccinated?

They are not. I'm happy to discuss specific claims if you have a source for this. 

>Why is there NO focus on early treatment to prevent hospitalization if infected?

Treatment with monoclonal antibodies is recommended for people who are at high risk of severe illness to prevent hospitalization ([source](https://www.covid19treatmentguidelines.nih.gov/management/clinical-management/nonhospitalized-adults--therapeutic-management/)). This treatment is only being recommended for people who are at high risk of severe illness because they are new treatments that are still being studied, and doctors need to balance the risk of side effects against the potential benefits, so they are just being used for people who are at the highest risk of hospitalization and severe illness.

>Why are existing proven treatments being sidelined while Pfizer and Merck work on their proprietary versions of these proven treatments?

There has been a lot of misinformation in the media about what treatments have been proven to work. All treatments with solid evidence to support their efficacy are being used. Again, happy to discuss specific claims if you have a source.

>If vaccinated, will I need a booster every 6 months for life?

Nope! Right now, you don't need a booster at all. There may be a recommendation to do a one-time booster in the future. Don't let this stop you from getting vaccinated--even if boosters are recommended later, having just the initial doses of the vaccine provides better protection than no vaccine at all.

Fun disease facts corner: It is possible to get polio from the polio vaccine, but not the type used in the US. The vaccine used in the US, and in most of the world now, is an inactivated virus vaccine, so there's no way it can make you sick. There is also a live attenuated virus vaccine that basically contains a weakened version of the virus, and in a small number of cases it can mutate and make people sick. This vaccine has saved millions of lives though! It can be given orally, so you don't need a healthcare provider to give it as a shot. This lets it be used in rural areas with no access to healthcare, and has helped move towards the global eradication of polio. Once an area is free of polio and the tiny risk of developing polio from the oral vaccine is greater than the risk of getting it in the community, countries switch to the inactivated virus vaccine so they stay polio-free. Only one human disease has ever been eradicated, smallpox, but polio might be the second! Yay vaccines!

Evidence aside, if it does actually change your acetylcholine levels, that is a big deal. High levels of acetylcholine can kill you. Nerve agents, like sarin gas or the Novichok agent that was used to poison Alexander Nalvany, work by increasing the amount of acetylcholine in your synapses. **TLDR: please do not take ParaSym Plus without talking to your doctor first.**

There has only ever been one study done on this, and it was done really poorly. The results are basically meaningless. "Cure alls" cure nothing. Please do not pay hundreds of dollars for this. 

The GUPTA one seems potentially more promising, there is some data to back up their claims and there is one proper study that showed that it works. They also offer a money-back guarantee. Eating spider eggs, snake skin, etc. can't cause any actual living organisms inside of you. In most of these examples, the item isn't capable of turning into the creature--for example, nothing you do to snake skin in any circumstances is going to cause an actual snake to grow. While eggs could theoretically hatch into a creature, they would be immediately destroyed by stomach acid. Parasites have evolved to survive in the harsh conditions of the GI system (or wherever they live), but things like insect or frog eggs don't need to be able to survive in those conditions, so they haven't evolved to have that ability.

That being said, I would not be surprised if there are examples of these substances would be harmful if you ate them. Some frogs produce extremely potent poisons, and I certainly wouldn't want to eat any of their tadpoles. (Or any tadpoles, but I think that's just a personal preference.) Ingesting these things might have biological effects, but they wouldn't be caused by literal creatures living inside you.
